summary: VRM is a humanoid avatar format built on glTF 2.0: a VRM file is a binary glTF file with one added extension and a changed file suffix, so everything the base format settles about meshes, textures and skins is inherited unchanged. What VRM adds is the part that makes an avatar work in a place it was not made for, and the base format has none of it: a fixed set of 55 named human bones with fixed parentage, 15 of them required; a normative rest pose that fixes which way the model faces and puts the soles on the ground plane at zero; and 18 named facial expressions covering five moods, five mouth shapes for speech, three eye closings and four gaze directions. It also carries permission data, which no other asset format on this map does, with required author names, a required link to the VRM Public License, and eleven machine-readable settings covering who may wear the model, commercial use, credit, modification, redistribution and violent, sexual, political or hateful content, every one of them defaulting to the restrictive value. Three traps for a standards audience: the expression names are agreed but the faces are not, because the specification says plainly that there is no specification for the facial deformation itself, so the same named expression need not look alike on two models; a VRM file carries no animation at all, because the core declares the base format's animation and camera arrays unused and puts humanoid motion in a separate file defined by a separate extension; and there is nothing for worn items, no attachment point, no socket and no way to reference a second file, so clothing has to be baked into the avatar mesh before export. Version 1.0 is the current one, released in September 2022; the older 0.x line used a different and incompatible extension key and is now deprecated.

coverage.note: This is the subject: a portable humanoid avatar carried as a binary glTF file with the VRMC_vrm extension and the .vrm suffix.

coverage.note: The strongest part of VRM and the thing the base format lacks: 55 named human bones in five tables, 15 of them required, each with a fixed parent and a stated rule for skipping absent parents, plus a normative rest pose fixing the facing direction, the ground plane and the finger orientations.

Custom names are allowed but may not reuse a preset name. The trap is that only the names are agreed, not the faces.

What is missing is normative force for the hard part: the rules for reconciling models with different rest rotations and different optional bones sit in a document the project marks as non-normative.

coverage.note: VRM defines no worn item, no attachment point and no socket. Clothing, hats and held props must be part of the avatar's own mesh hierarchy before export; the only thing an implementation can hang an item on is the named bone set, and nothing in the specification says how. The spring bone extension mentions costumes only as something that should sway.

coverage.note: No reduced avatar representation of any kind. The nearest thing, the first-person mesh annotation, switches whole meshes on and off per camera to keep the wearer's own head out of their view; it does not reduce detail and does not help with crowds or weak devices.

sources.title: VRMC_vrm 1.0 specification
sources.quote: Saved in `.glb` format and using `.vrm` as the extension.

coverage.note: Binding and skinning are glTF's; the part VRM adds is the mapping from each named human bone to a glTF node, which is what makes the rig readable by a runtime that never saw the model. Bone transforms are constrained further: scale must be uniform and positive.

sources.title: VRMC_vrm.humanoid
sources.quote: For transforms of humanoid bones, scale components MUST have positive values (zero is not permitted).

sources.title: VRM T-pose
sources.quote: All node transforms must be in a positive uniform scale.

coverage.note: The shape deformation itself is glTF's morph targets, which VRM does not change. What VRM adds is naming: expressions bind groups of morph targets to an agreed name, and because glTF has no name for a morph target the specification recommends putting one in the mesh extras. Missing: VRM specifies no encoding of its own.

sources.title: VRMC_vrm 1.0 specification, names of morphTargets

coverage.note: A VRM file carries no animation: the core says the glTF animations and cameras arrays are not used. Humanoid motion lives in a separate file defined by VRMC_vrm_animation 1.0, which reuses glTF's own keyframe machinery and adds the mapping to named bones, expressions and gaze.

coverage.note: Mesh encoding is glTF's and VRM specifies none of it. What VRM adds is two restrictions aimed at making models load the same everywhere: stored tangents may be left out and recalculated, and morph target tangents should be neither exported nor imported.

coverage.note: Image encoding is glTF's. VRM adds one restriction and it is a narrow one: the model thumbnail must be square and must be a jpg or png supported by glTF's core, with extension formats forbidden. Missing: nothing is said about texture compression for the model's own textures.

coverage.note: Handedness and axis order come from glTF and VRM restates none of it. VRM does add the convention glTF lacks for characters: in the rest pose the model stands facing positive Z, symmetrical about X, arms out along X, and every node scale must be uniform and positive. Missing: no transform convention of its own beyond the rest pose.

coverage.note: Metric scale is inherited from glTF. VRM adds the rule that makes avatar size and grounding usable: the sole surface sits on the plane at Y zero in appearance, so a receiving world can place the feet and read the height without guessing where the ankle bone is. Missing: the unit agreement itself is glTF's.

coverage.note: Unusual for a 3D format and the reason VRM matters to the rights columns. The meta block requires a name, at least one author and a licence document link that must point at the VRM Public License, and then adds eleven machine-readable settings: who may act as this avatar, commercial use, credit, redistribution, modification, and flags for violent, sexual, political or religious, and antisocial or hateful use. coverage.note: A VRM model keeps its glTF core material, so a plain physically based renderer will show something. What will not carry is the intended look: the toon material is defined by reference to particular rendering techniques, so shade colour, rim light, matcap and outline are reproduced only by a renderer that implements the extension.

coverage.note: A VRM file is one self-contained humanoid. There is no referencing another file, no layering and no override, which is the structural reason a wearable cannot be shipped separately from the avatar it is worn on.

sources.title: VRMC_materials_mtoon 1.0

coverage.note: VRM removes glTF cameras from use, then defines the one viewpoint an avatar needs: the wearer's own. Meshes are annotated third person only, first person only, both or auto, and the auto rule splits a mesh by head bone weight so the wearer does not see the inside of their own face. Missing: no camera definition, no viewpoint binding, no way to move between viewpoints.

coverage.note: Collision shapes exist but serve one purpose only. VRMC_springBone defines sphere and capsule colliders, and VRMC_springBone_extended_collider adds inside sphere, inside capsule and plane with a stated fallback for readers that do not know them. Missing: these are read only by the spring solver; there is no general contact test and no collision geometry for the body itself.

sources.title: VRMC_springBone_extended_collider 1.0

coverage.note: VRMC_springBone 1.0 gives hair and clothing their swing, with stiffness, drag and gravity per joint and a written update procedure. Missing: it is a chain of bones, not a deformable simulation. There is no cloth solver, no mesh deformation, branching chains are undefined, and two runtimes stepping at different rates will not match.

coverage.note: The terms travel with the file in a form a program can read, which is the hard half and the half almost nobody does. Missing is the acting half: the settings are unsigned, no protocol checks them, nothing binds a receiving world to honour them, and the licence text they refer to is enforced by law rather than by the format.

sources.title: VRMC_vrm 1.0 specification
sources.quote: Written against the glTF 2.0 spec.

coverage.note: VRM is a file format for humanoid 3D avatars built on glTF. It defines bone mapping, expression blendshapes, spring physics, look-at, and first-person rendering. It has no scene hosting concept and no containment model.

sources.title: VRMC_vrm 1.0 specification
sources.quote: VRM is a file format for handling 3D humanoid avatar data for VR applications.

coverage.note: VRM is an avatar format. It carries no networking, no world state, and no mechanism for inter-world coupling. State changes between worlds are outside the format's scope.

sources.title: VRMC_vrm 1.0 specification
sources.quote: VRM is a file format for handling 3D humanoid avatar data for VR applications.

coverage.note: VRM carries a humanoid avatar on top of glTF. It defines no exchange in which a payer receives payment requirements, authorizes and gets a settlement result.

sources.title: VRMC_vrm-1.0 specification
sources.quote: glTF represent an entire Scene, whereas VRM represent a Humanoid for VR avatar.

coverage.note: VRM 1.0 declares who may use a model as an avatar and says a paid model needs a separate licence, but defines no grant, holder binding, expiry, revocation or check. Searched VRMC_vrm-1.0 README and meta.md, VRMC_springBone-1.0, VRMC_materials_mtoon-1.0, VRMC_node_constraint-1.0 and VRMC_vrm_animation-1.0 (vrm-specification master, commit 94e82dd) for entitle, purchase, paid, authoriz, authentic, revok, expir, DRM, signature and encrypt on 2026-10-20; the only hit is the licence value quoted here.
